articles.summary: Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz threaten fertilizer and diesel supplies, sparking fears of a global food crisis  재경일보
articles.full_text:
Analysis suggests that an energy supply shock triggered by a US-Iran war could burden the global food market by extending into shortages of fertilizer and agricultural diesel. If combined with a strong El Niño, causing both rising production costs and poor harvests, the pressure on food prices could materialize in full by 2027.
Disruptions in fertilizer raw material supply due to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz
As the US-Iran war blocks transit through the Strait of Hormuz, the supply of fertilizer and raw materials essential for agriculture is faltering. This strait is a major maritime corridor for crude oil and liquefied natural gas, as well as substances used in fertilizer production such as urea, ammonia, and sulfur. S&P Global analyzed that the Persian Gulf region supplies nearly half of the world's traded sulfur, and that roughly 29% of global urea trade, nearly half of sulfur trade, and about 21% of seaborne ammonia trade pass through the Strait of Hormuz. The price of sulfur, a raw material for fertilizer, rose by approximately 70% in September compared to January of this year. If fertilizer prices rise, farmers may reduce input quantities or cut back on cultivation areas. In this case, the burden of production costs increases immediately, but the decrease in yields and the contraction of food supply appear after the next harvest, meaning market shocks may be reflected with a lag.

articles.title: Powering Korea’s AI ambitions: Latin America’s rising role in critical minerals to 2030 - BNamericas
articles.summary: Powering Korea’s AI ambitions: Latin America’s rising role in critical minerals to 2030  BNamericas
articles.full_text:
South Korea imports more than 95% of the minerals its technology industry needs, and that dependence will grow with the semiconductor, AI and data center megaprojects Seoul is preparing. Latin America, and Chile in particular, is central to that strategy.
Wonseok Choi, chief representative in Chile of the state-owned Korea Mine Rehabilitation and Mineral Resources Corporation (KOMIR), closely follows copper, lithium and rare earth developments in the region.
In an interview with BNamericas, Choi discusses mining partners, the region’s role toward 2030 and KOMIR’s experience in mine closure.
Copper, molybdenum and lithium: Chile’s hand
BNamericas: With South Korea importing more than 95% of the minerals that power its technology industry, which Latin American country do you expect to become its most important mining trade partner over the next decade, and why?
Choi: Over the next decade, I see Chile as the strongest candidate, especially for copper and lithium. The trading relationship is already substantial. According to Chile’s official figures, its 2025 exports to Korea included about US$1.87bn in copper ore and concentrates and US$969mn in copper cathodes. Lithium carbonate exports exceeded US$300mn. In June, the Korean government announced three mega-projects in semiconductors, physical AI and data centers. As they develop, demand will grow for copper in data center power grids, molybdenum in chip wiring and equipment, and lithium in robot batteries, and Chile supplies all three.
That assessment does depend on the minerals covered and the scope of the trade figures. If all minerals are included, Brazil’s iron ore trade weighs heavily, while Mexico and Peru remain major suppliers of copper, zinc and other metals. Argentina’s lithium trade could grow substantially, supported by new production capacity and Korean investments, including POSCO’s Sal de Oro project. Bolivia’s longer-term contribution will depend on how individual projects and its investment framework develop.
With Korea’s high import dependence for metallic minerals, diversification needs to be accompanied by resilience: the ability to keep industry operating through export restrictions or disruptions to logistics. We should maintain Chile as a key partner while developing complementary relationships with other countries in the region, on sound commercial terms.
The common challenge: turning policies into projects
BNamericas: Chile, Argentina, Peru and Bolivia are each adapting their mining policies to growing demand for critical minerals. What is the biggest gap each one still needs to close to attract long-term investment?
Choi: Each country’s policy reflects its own production base and institutions. Through its lithium and critical minerals strategies, Chile aims to sustain its mining base, develop other minerals and add more value locally. Its main challenges are the time and cost of meeting project requirements and maintaining output at aging mines. Argentina is attracting large investments through RIGI, which offers approved projects long-term tax, customs and foreign-exchange stability, although infrastructure and coordination with provincial governments remain important.
Peru is working to turn its large project portfolio into actual investment, which depends on permitting, infrastructure and lasting relationships with local communities. Bolivia has large lithium resources but limited production, and has proposed a new lithium law to improve legal certainty and transparency.
There are common goals too. All four countries want to attract foreign investment while keeping more value at home. They compete for the same capital, but also cooperate more. In August, they signed a joint declaration on strategic minerals, and Chile and Argentina are using their mining integration treaty for cross-border projects.
The next task is implementation. Investors need predictable permitting, while communities need to know how environmental impacts will be managed and what jobs and business opportunities a project will bring. These issues should be discussed early, and governments and companies must keep their commitments. Each project that moves forward this way makes the next investment easier. To benefit from growing demand, countries must be able to turn policies into projects.
Toward 2030: more minerals, more value added
BNamericas: Where do Chile and Latin America stand today in the global minerals supply chain?
Choi: Latin America is central to global copper and lithium supply, with large reserves and an established production base. It is also an important partner for Korean industry, supplying copper from Chile and Peru, lithium from Chile and niobium from Brazil, while POSCO is producing lithium in Argentina. That is why Latin America is always part of Korea’s discussions on diversifying mineral supplies.
By 2030, I expect the region’s role to expand both in the range of minerals it supplies and across the value chain. Beyond copper and lithium, Brazil offers opportunities to increase supplies of rare earths, graphite and nickel. Across the region, efforts to move from raw materials to processed materials will continue. Suppliers that can demonstrate their environmental performance and provide traceable production records will also become more important. Chile is pursuing this direction through its National Mining Policy 2050, National Lithium Strategy and National Critical Minerals Strategy.
In copper, I am watching the ‘copper triangle’ of Chile, Peru and Argentina, which CESCO has highlighted this year. Combining Chile and Peru’s established production bases with Argentina’s development potential could strengthen the region’s role in supplying copper for power grids and electrification. Not every new project will enter production by 2030, but progress toward development over the next few years will also shape global supply beyond that date.
In rare earths, I am following projects in Brazil and Chile. The emergence of a new production base in Latin America is significant in a market where supply is concentrated in a few countries. Brazil is also running an industrial demonstration project, MagBras, to connect domestic rare earth production with permanent magnet manufacturing. If those links can be established, Latin America could play a larger role in supplying materials for advanced manufacturing.
AI, sensors and waste with value in mine closure
BNamericas: What technological innovations is KOMIR using to achieve more effective mine rehabilitation and closure?
Choi: Korea has more than 5,000 abandoned and idle mines, many without rehabilitation. KOMIR and its predecessor have spent about 20 years rehabilitating these sites with public funds. For mine drainage, the challenge is reliable long-term treatment at lower cost. At our largest treatment plant, an AI-based system adjusts chemical dosing to water quality, cleans sensors automatically and anticipates maintenance needs. With a Korean company, we are also developing solar-powered modular membrane systems that reduce the need for large settling ponds. Some treated water is already reused for firefighting, artificial snowmaking, dust control and crop irrigation.
Ground subsidence over abandoned underground workings is another major issue. Our MIRECO EYE system, certified as a new technology in Korea, lowers laser, sonar and imaging sensors through boreholes to produce 3D models of inaccessible underground cavities, which guide backfilling and reinforcement. We have also field-tested optical fiber sensors to detect small ground deformations.
We also seek to add value to waste. An adsorbent made from mine drainage sludge, which removes hydrogen sulfide from biogas, is certified as a New Environmental Technology and is already sold by a private company. The sludge is also being studied for removing arsenic and recovering metals from tailings.
On climate risk, KOMIR was the first Korean public institution to apply climate scenarios to the design and operation of mine reclamation facilities. We are also part of a national pilot project that fills abandoned mine shafts with carbonated slag, made by reacting steel slag with CO2, to store carbon and stabilize the ground. Long-term storage safety and environmental impacts are still being verified.

articles.title: QatarEnergy signs deal to buy 4 million tons of US LNG annually through 2054 - Anadolu Ajansı
articles.summary: QatarEnergy signs deal to buy 4 million tons of US LNG annually through 2054  Anadolu Ajansı
articles.full_text:
Sahin Demir
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
QatarEnergy announced Thursday that it signed two long-term agreements with US energy company Cheniere to purchase up to 4 million tons of liquefied natural gas (LNG) annually from facilities in Louisiana and Texas through 2054.
The agreements cover LNG supplies from Cheniere’s Sabine Pass facility in Louisiana and Corpus Christi facility in Texas, both located along the US Gulf Coast, QatarEnergy said in a statement.
Under the agreements, deliveries are expected to begin in 2031 and continue through 2054 on a free-on-board (FOB) basis, meaning QatarEnergy will take responsibility for the LNG shipments at the loading ports.
Cheniere said in a separate statement that QatarEnergy would purchase 2 million tons annually from each facility, with prices indexed to the US Henry Hub natural gas benchmark plus a fixed fee.
The US company added that 1 million tons annually under the Sabine Pass agreement would be subject to a positive final investment decision on the first phase of its planned expansion project.
The agreements were signed by Qatar’s Minister of State for Energy Affairs and QatarEnergy President and CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi and Cheniere Chairman, President and CEO Jack Fusco.
Al-Kaabi described the agreements as an important milestone in QatarEnergy’s LNG strategy.
“This major long-term purchase will expand and diversify our global LNG portfolio and advance our ability to meet the evolving requirements of the market,” he said.
He added that the additional volumes would complement QatarEnergy’s existing LNG supplies, strengthen its trading portfolio and enhance its ability to serve customers worldwide.
For his part, Fusco said the agreements represented a major long-term commercial commitment and reinforced Cheniere’s position in the US LNG industry.
The deal comes as QatarEnergy seeks to diversify its global LNG supply and trading portfolio while strengthening its position in international energy markets.
Cheniere operates the Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi LNG facilities, with a combined production capacity of approximately 56 million tons annually and additional capacity under construction.
The company is also developing an expansion of its Sabine Pass facility, which could increase the terminal’s total production capacity to more than 50 million tons annually.
The agreements come amid heightened tensions in the Middle East and disruptions to energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway connecting the Gulf with international markets.
Qatar, one of the world’s leading LNG exporters, relies heavily on maritime routes through the strait to deliver gas to customers in Asia and Europe.
The purchase of US-produced LNG is expected to provide QatarEnergy with additional supply options outside the Gulf, allowing it to diversify its trading portfolio and reduce its reliance on shipments originating from the region.

articles.title: QatarEnergy Signs 4 MTPA LNG Deal With Cheniere Through 2054 - Hoodline
articles.summary: QatarEnergy Signs 4 MTPA LNG Deal With Cheniere Through 2054  Hoodline
articles.full_text:
QatarEnergy has locked in a major new supply line of American natural gas, signing two long-term agreements with Cheniere to purchase up to 4 million tonnes per annum of liquefied natural gas from export terminals in Texas and Louisiana. The agreements run through 2054, arriving as Qatar's own LNG exports remain hobbled by regional shipping disruptions.
Two Deals, Two Gulf Coast Terminals
According to Qatar Tribune, the two sale and purchase agreements split the volume evenly, with Cheniere's Sabine Pass Liquefaction and Corpus Christi Liquefaction subsidiaries each supplying 2 million tonnes per annum on a free-on-board basis, as reported by BIC Magazine. Under that FOB structure, QatarEnergy takes responsibility for the cargo once it is loaded at the export terminal, and pricing is indexed to Henry Hub plus a fixed fee. One million tonnes per annum tied to the Sabine Pass agreement is contingent on a positive final investment decision for the first phase of the Sabine Pass Expansion Project, per the same outlet.
Dossier sources diverge slightly on when the gas will start flowing. Qatar Tribune reports deliveries are anticipated to begin in 2031 and continue through 2054, while BIC Magazine describes deliveries beginning in the early 2030s and running through the end of 2054. Either way, the agreements lock in decades of supply for QatarEnergy's portfolio.
Who Signed, and What They Said
The agreements were signed by Saad Sherida Al Kaabi, Qatar's Minister of State for Energy Affairs and QatarEnergy's President and CEO, along with Jack Fusco, Chairman, President and CEO of Cheniere Energy, according to Trend News Agency. Al Kaabi said the agreements marked an important milestone in QatarEnergy's LNG strategy, adding that the purchase will expand and diversify the company's global LNG portfolio and improve its ability to meet changing market requirements, Trend reported. The added volumes are expected to complement QatarEnergy's existing supplies, strengthen its supply and trading portfolio, and enhance its ability to serve customers worldwide, while Cheniere gains a long-term sales framework for the LNG produced at its U.S. export facilities, per the same report.
War Disruptions Reshape Qatar's Export Picture
The timing underscores why Doha is looking west for supply. QatarEnergy has been forced to dramatically reduce flows as shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains in turmoil, and the country's Ras Laffan facility was damaged during the war, according to Bloomberg. QatarEnergy restored LNG exports in September to about a third of prewar levels, Bloomberg reported as cited by Semafor, which also noted that at least 20 more shipments have passed through the Strait of Hormuz to other destinations since early September.
QatarEnergy has a broader strategy of diversifying its LNG procurement sources and maintaining a flexible supply portfolio, Trend reported, and this deal fits that pattern even as the company works to stabilize its own production.
Cheniere's Expanding Gulf Coast Footprint
Cheniere's two liquefaction complexes on the Gulf Coast give it the scale to absorb the new commitment. Sabine Pass in Louisiana has six fully operational liquefaction trains, each capable of producing approximately 5 million tonnes per annum, with trains brought online ahead of schedule and within budget, according to Trend. The facility carries roughly 30 million tonnes per annum of aggregate nominal production capacity and can draw natural gas from every supply source in the continental United States east of the Rocky Mountains, working with dozens of producers and infrastructure companies to move gas to the terminal.
Corpus Christi Liquefaction, located along the north shore of Corpus Christi Bay in San Patricio County, Texas, has 10 fully operational liquefaction trains and three containment tanks each holding 160,000 cubic meters of LNG storage capacity, per Trend. The site has two berths capable of receiving Q-Max carriers, the largest class of LNG ship, which measure 344.4 meters long and carry 266,000 cubic meters of cargo. Cheniere's investor relations team has described the combined Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi platform as having approximately 56 million tonnes per annum of operating production capacity, a figure released alongside the company's announcement of substantial completion for the Corpus Christi Liquefaction Stage 3 project in late August. Reuters has separately reported Cheniere's present capacity at 52 million tonnes per annum with another 8 million tonnes per annum under construction, while Stocktitan cited roughly 56 million tonnes per annum in operation plus about 5 million tonnes per annum under construction — figures that differ depending on the source.
More Growth on the Horizon
Cheniere is not standing still on expansion. The company signed its engineering, procurement and construction contract with Bechtel Energy for the first phase of the Sabine Pass Expansion Project in May 2026, according to Stocktitan. That expansion is expected to add up to roughly 20 million tonnes per annum of peak production capacity, pushing total Sabine Pass capacity past 50 million tonnes per annum, per BIC Magazine's reporting.
Cheniere has also applied to build a separate, 24 million-metric-ton-per-year LNG plant at its Corpus Christi site, which would add four new trains producing 6 million tonnes per annum apiece and raise the facility's eventual capacity to 49 million tonnes per annum, according to Reuters. The U.S. exported 111 million metric tonnes of LNG in 2025, per preliminary LSEG data cited by Reuters, and the Energy Information Administration has projected that the country's export capacity could nearly double by 2031 compared with December 2025, per the agency's own analysis. The QatarEnergy-Cheniere agreements add one more long-term buyer to that growing pipeline of American gas heading overseas.

articles.title: QatarEnergy Eyes 3 Million Tonnes of US LNG in Venture Global Deal - ChemAnalyst
articles.summary: QatarEnergy Eyes 3 Million Tonnes of US LNG in Venture Global Deal  ChemAnalyst
articles.full_text:
Welcome To ChemAnalyst
	QatarEnergy is in advanced talks with US liquefied natural gas (LNG) producer Venture Global to secure at least 3 million metric tonnes of LNG annually under a potential long-term supply agreement, according to several media reports. The proposed deal could strengthen QatarEnergy’s access to US gas supplies as disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continue to affect regional energy flows.
	According to several media reports, QatarEnergy has been purchasing LNG from Venture Global through the spot market to meet some of its customers’ requirements. Shipping constraints linked to the US-Israeli war on Iran and Tehran’s retaliatory strikes this year have sharply curtailed maritime traffic through the strategic waterway, prompting QatarEnergy to seek alternative supply arrangements.
	The timeline for a potential agreement and the duration of any contract remain unclear. However, a long-term deal could provide QatarEnergy with greater flexibility in managing supply commitments while reducing its dependence on immediately available spot cargoes during periods of market disruption.
	Venture Global is currently the US LNG supplier with the largest volume of uncommitted capacity, positioning the company to accommodate additional long-term supply agreements. Its export capacity could expand further when the CP2 LNG facility, currently under construction in Louisiana, begins production. The project could help Venture Global become the second-largest LNG exporter in the United States.
	The potential agreement would also mark another significant development in QatarEnergy’s efforts to secure US LNG supplies through long-term contracts. On Thursday, Cheniere Energy, the largest US LNG exporter, announced a long-term agreement to supply QatarEnergy with 4 million metric tonnes per annum (mtpa) from 2031 to 2054.
	Under the Cheniere agreement, 2 mtpa will come from the Sabine Pass facility in Louisiana, while the remaining 2 mtpa will be supplied from the Corpus Christi terminal in Texas. The deal provides QatarEnergy with a substantial volume of contracted LNG from US export infrastructure over an extended period.
	If finalised, the proposed Venture Global agreement would further diversify QatarEnergy’s supply portfolio and deepen commercial ties between the Qatari energy company and US LNG producers. For Venture Global, the arrangement could secure a major long-term customer, improve revenue visibility and support future export capacity utilisation.
	The negotiations highlight how geopolitical risks and shipping disruptions are influencing LNG procurement strategies. Buyers are increasingly balancing spot-market flexibility with long-term contracts to protect supply security and manage exposure to volatile international gas prices.
	Impact on LNG Supply and Chemical Commodity Prices
A long-term agreement could strengthen QatarEnergy’s LNG procurement security while providing Venture Global with more predictable demand and supporting future US export capacity. Additional contracted volumes may reduce QatarEnergy’s reliance on spot purchases during shipping disruptions, although the proposed deal’s timing and duration remain unconfirmed. For chemical markets, sustained LNG availability could support natural gas supplies used in ammonia, methanol and other gas-intensive production. However, LNG prices may remain elevated if Strait of Hormuz disruptions persist or global cargo competition intensifies. Any impact on ammonia, methanol, urea and related commodity prices will depend on regional gas costs, freight rates and supply-demand balances.

- Algo Grande Copper Corp.'s Adelita project in Sonora, Mexico, is a copper-silver-gold project in the Arizona-Sonora copper belt, putting it in the two metals Moriarty says are short.c

- S&P Global projects copper demand will rise 50% by 2040, with a supply shortfall of about 10 million metric tons.
The Golden Age of Mining
Veteran resource investor Bob Moriarty of 321gold.com says mining is about to enter a "golden age," and the metals in shortest supply are copper and silver. In a recent interview with host Gary Bohm on the Metals and Miners podcast, the founder of 321gold said copper is "definitely in shortage" and silver is as well. Gold is not, he argued, because the world has about an 80-year supply of it sitting above ground.
Moriarty said the mining industry has been devastated over the last 20 years, and the major producers stopped exploring. Now, he said, those majors are starting to pick up juniors that are doing the exploration and finding big projects. Bohm noted that capital has largely stayed away from mining since 2011, leaving exploration budgets and new large discoveries at their lowest levels in decades, even as demand builds from AI, robotics, the military, and grid expansion.
Governments are stepping in to fill the gap. Bohm pointed out that the United States is now investing directly in mining companies. Moriarty said he welcomes the support, even though he generally opposes government involvement in the economy, and argued that miners would do far better if governments stopped standing in their way.
The Bull Case for Commodities
Moriarty covered a wide range of topics in the interview. Among his key points:
- Copper and silver are in shortage, but gold is not, thanks to decades of above-ground supply.
- Demand for silver from solar power, electronics, and the solid-state silver batteries Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd (005930:KRX) has developed could send the price sharply higher.
- The majors stopped exploring and are now buying juniors that find large projects.
- Only about 2% of the entire financial marketplace is in commodities, setting up a boom across everything from copper and silver to wheat and corn.
- There is no shortage of tungsten, but China controls the price by restricting exports, so companies that can reach production within two to three years should do well.
- Rare earth elements aren't actually rare, and the real bottleneck is processing them into usable metals.
- With U.S. debt at US$40 trillion and unlikely to be repaid, more inflation is unavoidable.
A Crash Could Open the Door
Moriarty believes the broader stock market is already in the early stages of a crash, driven by an AI bubble that he said is bursting. When margin calls hit, he said, investors sell what they can, not what they want to, and that will drag some of the best mining stocks down to absurdly low levels. He called it "the opportunity of a lifetime."
Gold and silver stocks will likely fall with the rest of the market, Moriarty said, but they will be the first to recover. He said he has never seen so many good companies with strong management and projects in demand selling so cheaply. Investors who already own them can ride it out, he said, while those holding cash should be ready to buy quality stocks at fair value.
Bohm added that efforts to reshore supply chains away from China are costly and are setting up competition for the same natural resources, which favors hard assets with pricing power. That could benefit North American projects close to the manufacturers that need the metals.

Algo Grande's first drill program at the Cerro Grande skarn, four holes totaling 1,998 meters, confirmed what the company called "an outcropping, vertically extensive, multi-horizon skarn system," with "increasing evidence supporting a genetically related porphyry system at depth," according to its April 2 release. Porphyry systems are the source of most of the world's copper.
Location matters too. As the United States works to bring critical mineral supply chains closer to home, a copper-silver project in North America fits the reshoring push Bohm described.
Phase II Pays Off
Algo Grande began its Phase II program of about 8,000 meters in June. The program aims to expand the Cerro Grande discovery along a 2.5-kilometer corridor and to drill the Cerro Potrero South and Las Trancas targets for the first time.
In September, the company closed an oversubscribed private placement of 7,977,497 shares at CA$0.60 each for gross proceeds of about CA$4.79 million, money earmarked for continued drilling and exploration at Adelita.
The first Phase II assays came soon after. On September 11, the company reported that hole AG-CG-PH2-002 cut 30.23 meters grading 1.5% copper equivalent (CuEq), including 3.55 meters at 9.4% CuEq and 1.2 meters at 15.8% CuEq.
On September 23, deeper results from the same hole added a new zone of 38.20 meters at 1.0% CuEq, including 11.50 meters at 2.0% CuEq. That brings the hole's total to 68.43 meters of copper-silver-gold mineralization across two zones. All intervals are downhole lengths, and true widths haven't been determined.
On September 30, Algo Grande secured a five-year surface access agreement with the Ejido Palos Chinos community covering about 1,796 hectares at Adelita. The agreement allows mapping, sampling, geophysical surveys, and drilling through September 2031.
Gravity Points the Way
The next round of news is already in motion. Assays are pending from hole AG-CG-PH2-003, which intersected fault-hosted skarn with visible copper minerals at a target separate from Cerro Grande, the company said on October 7. The same release said core testing showed mineralized skarn is noticeably denser than the surrounding rock. Algo Grande plans to use that difference in a ground gravity survey, which was set to begin on October 22 across a 7-kilometer limestone corridor. The survey covers about 1,296 stations and should take 28 to 35 field days, with a final report expected about seven weeks after fieldwork ends.
The company also plans an induced polarization calibration test over known mineralization at Cerro Grande before extending that survey to new gravity targets. The results will help guide where the next phase of drilling goes.
"Magnetics finds the structure, gravity finds the weight, IP finds the charge," Chief Executive Officer Enrico Gay said.
Betting on a Big Find
Moriarty has followed Algo Grande since early on. In a September 14 commentary, written before the deeper Hole 2 results arrived, he pointed to the hole's high-grade 3.55-meter interval and said the drilling to date suggests the potential for a district-scale find.
"I have believed since I was first informed about the company that they had the potential for a giant discovery," he wrote, adding that the shares looked significantly undervalued.
He also noted that Sonora produces about 80% of Mexico's copper. "The world needs more copper. A great deal more," Moriarty wrote in a June 16 Streetwise Reports contributor opinion.

articles.full_text:
Halo Minerals (AIM: HALO) has secured a key mining permit for its Playa Verde copper-gold tailings project in Chile, advancing plans to recover metal from historic mine waste as global demand for copper accelerates.
The permit allows Halo’s subsidiary Minera Playa Verde to dredge mineral-bearing material from Chañaral beach, including within the urban area. Chile’s Ministry of Housing and Urban Development (MINVU) raised no objections to the authorization, removing a regulatory hurdle as the company works towards a final investment decision, the company said.
“The granting of this permit represents another important milestone in the advancement of Playa Verde and continues the progress we are making across the Project’s permitting and development workstreams,” Halo CEO Andrew Dennan said.
The project offers an alternative to conventional copper mining by extracting valuable metals from existing tailings while treating material accumulated along the coastline. The approach could help developers tap overlooked sources of supply without relying entirely on new mines, which often face lengthy permitting and construction timelines.
One man’s trash, another’s treasure
Playa Verde is designed to process about 5 million tonnes of mineral-bearing material annually, producing an estimated 8,600 tonnes of payable copper in cathodes and concentrates. Halo projects annual cash flow of approximately $50 million.
The operation would use dredging equipment to recover historic tailings deposited at Chañaral before transporting the material to a metallurgical processing plant.
“Playa Verde presents an opportunity to recover copper from historic mine tailings while treating and conditioning material that has accumulated on the beach at Chañaral,” Dennan said. “We believe this combination of copper production and environmental benefits differentiates Playa Verde and reinforces its potential to become a responsibly developed source of copper.”
The permit marks progress, but the project has yet to reach a final investment decision.
Growing supply gap
The approval comes as the mining industry faces a widening gap between projected copper demand and future mine supply, driven partly by electrification, renewable energy infrastructure and artificial intelligence.
Global copper consumption is forecast to climb 61% between 2026 and 2050 to nearly 46 million tonnes annually, potentially leaving a supply shortfall of 20 million tonnes, equivalent to 44% of projected demand.
The rapid expansion of data centres adds another source of pressure. BHP estimates copper demand from data centres could increase sixfold by 2050, while a single hyperscale AI facility can require as much as 50,000 tonnes of the metal, compared with 5,000 to 15,000 tonnes for a conventional installation.
Dennan argues that the mining industry’s traditional response to rising consumption — developing new deposits — overlooks opportunities to recover metals from waste generated by decades of previous production.
An estimated 282 billion tonnes of mine tailings exist worldwide, representing a potentially significant secondary source of critical minerals. However, the economic viability of individual recovery projects depends on factors including metal grades, processing costs and environmental requirements.

Kodal Minerals (LON: KOD) is looking to expand its lithium business beyond its producing Bougouni mine in Mali, targeting a new discovery in Ghana as recovering prices improve the outlook for the battery metal.
The miner signed a binding agreement this week with GH Geo-Consult Ltd to earn up to an 80% interest in the Asamankese lithium project in Ghana’s Eastern Region. Kodal acquired an initial 10% stake for $300,000 and plans to invest at least $13 million over five years in exploration of the 156-sq.-km greenfield property.
“We understand the legislation, we understand how to work with local communities and authorities, and we believe the geological potential is very strong,” CEO Bernard Aylward told Reuters, referring to West Africa, where Kodal has operated for nearly two decades.
The expansion comes as West Africa, one of the world’s leading gold-producing regions, seeks to attract more investment in critical minerals. Governments are looking to diversify their mining sectors and capture greater economic benefits from growing demand for lithium and other battery materials.
Kodal’s Bougouni lithium mine, a joint venture with China’s Hainan, began production in 2025. The company also holds gold exploration assets in Mali and Ivory Coast, giving it an established regional presence as it pursues opportunities in battery metals.
Ghana exploration
Early exploration at Asamankese has identified promising pegmatite formations, with rock-chip samples returning grades of up to 3.02% lithium oxide (Li₂O) at the Amantra and Nfranta prospects.
The company sees similarities between the property’s early geological results and those recorded during the initial exploration stages at Bougouni, raising hopes that Ghana could host another significant lithium discovery.
“Asamankese represents a strategic expansion of Kodal’s lithium footprint in West Africa and provides an exciting new growth opportunity in Ghana,” Aylward said in a company statement.
Kodal is refining exploration targets ahead of reconnaissance diamond drilling at Asamankese, with the results guiding the scope and pace of further investment.
Aylward said the company intends to finance the work through existing cash reserves and operating cash flow from Bougouni rather than raising fresh equity.
The strategy comes as recovering lithium prices revive interest in new mine development following a prolonged downturn that delayed projects across the industry, including Ghana’s flagship Ewoyaa lithium project.
Aylward said demand from electric vehicles, energy storage systems and consumer electronics continues to underpin the long-term outlook for the metal.
Regional risks
Despite the geological potential, security remains a concern for mining companies operating in parts of West Africa.
Islamist militants have expanded their operations across central West Africa’s mining regions, challenging government control and raising concerns about the safety of personnel and investments.
Kodal has faced security challenges at Bougouni, where last year a guard was killed in an armed attack.
The risks have not deterred mining companies from pursuing opportunities in the region, where established gold operations and under-explored critical mineral deposits continue to attract investment.

articles.full_text:
Key Highlights
- Stock Performance: Faraday Copper Corp shares pulled back notably, closing down -8.26% on October 22, 2026.
- Developer Sentiment: Pre-revenue copper companies faced selling as investors reduced exposure to long-duration resource projects.
- Project Stage: Copper Creek remains in an active drilling phase, meaning valuation is driven by expectations rather than cash flow.
- Strategic Expansion: The recently completed acquisition of the San Manuel property from BHP enlarges the asset base but brings new study, permitting and funding demands.
Introduction
Faraday Copper Corp (TSX:FDY) is a Vancouver-based, exploration-stage copper company advancing the Copper Creek project in Arizona, which it owns outright. The project sits roughly 80 road kilometres northeast of Tucson and about 19 kilometres northeast of the town of San Manuel, within one of the most established copper regions in the United States. The company describes Copper Creek as one of the largest undeveloped copper projects in North America. A mineral resource estimate and a preliminary economic assessment have been completed, and a Phase IV drilling program has been underway since September 2025. In October 2026, Faraday completed the acquisition of the neighbouring San Manuel property from BHP, taking over ownership and operatorship, with BHP becoming a shareholder holding a stake of about 30% in the company. Faraday is now responsible for future studies, permitting and stakeholder engagement at San Manuel and plans to redevelop it alongside Copper Creek.
Despite these building blocks, the shares fell sharply during the session as copper-linked developers lost favour. Companies without production or revenue rely on investor confidence in future project value, and that confidence is highly responsive to shifts in copper sentiment, financing conditions and broader risk appetite. When markets turn defensive, developers like Faraday often see faster and deeper corrections than producing miners, because their valuations hinge on long-term assumptions about metal prices, permitting timelines and the capital needed to build a mine.
Key Reasons Behind Decline
The session's weakness appears to reflect several interconnected pressures on early-stage copper equities.
- Cooling Appetite for Copper Developers: Copper has been supported by long-term electrification and grid investment themes, yet sentiment toward developers can shift abruptly. When traders take profits or reduce speculative exposure, pre-production names tend to bear a disproportionate share of selling.
- Copper Price Hesitation: Changing expectations for industrial demand, particularly from major consuming economies, can introduce volatility into copper futures. For a developer, even modest price softness can alter perceived project economics and implied valuation.
- Funding and Dilution Considerations: Large-scale drilling programs and further technical studies require ongoing capital. Investors are often wary of future equity raises in weaker markets, which can prompt pre-emptive selling in exploration-stage shares.
- Integration of a Larger Portfolio: The San Manuel transaction, completed earlier in October, expands the company's opportunity set, but market participants may be weighing the study work, permitting effort and future spending that a two-project district strategy will demand, as well as how the new shareholder structure may evolve.
- Macro and Geopolitical Uncertainty: Global geopolitical tensions, trade and tariff uncertainty and energy-market volatility continue to cloud the outlook for industrial metals demand and mine construction costs, adding to caution across base metals equities.
Risks to Consider
Prospective investors should weigh the project's scale against several material risks:
- Exploration and Resource Risk: Drilling results may not expand or upgrade the resource as anticipated, and future estimates could differ from current expectations.
- Permitting and Development Timelines: Advancing a large copper project in Arizona involves federal, state and local approvals, and lengthy permitting processes can delay development decisions.
- Capital Intensity: Building a large copper mine requires substantial investment, and the company would need to secure significant financing or partnerships to move toward construction.
- Copper Market Volatility: Project economics are highly sensitive to long-term copper price assumptions, and a prolonged downturn could weaken the investment case.
- Redevelopment and Integration Risk: Redeveloping San Manuel alongside Copper Creek involves technical, environmental, regulatory and stakeholder challenges, and combining two projects into a coherent development plan may take longer or cost more than anticipated.
Valuation Perspective
From an analytical standpoint, Faraday is valued primarily on the potential of Copper Creek rather than on earnings or cash flow. Investors typically consider resource size, grade, project scale, infrastructure access and jurisdiction when assigning value to such developers. Arizona's established mining heritage and existing infrastructure are supportive features, but the absence of near-term production leaves valuation highly dependent on market sentiment.
The latest drop suggests that participants are applying a wider discount to long-dated copper development value. During risk-off sessions, the market tends to penalise companies whose path to production involves further drilling, studies, permitting and financing. Continued drilling success and progress on technical work could help rebuild confidence, while further weakness in copper sentiment or difficult funding conditions could keep the stock under pressure. The scale of capital required to eventually develop a project of this size also means that the market weighs potential partnership structures and dilution risk heavily when assessing value.
Outlook
Over the longer term, the structural demand story for copper, driven by electrification, renewable energy and grid modernisation, provides a supportive backdrop for large undeveloped projects in stable jurisdictions. Copper Creek's scale and location in a historically productive district, combined with the newly acquired San Manuel property and the involvement of a major global miner as a significant shareholder, give the company a platform that could become increasingly relevant as the industry looks for new supply.
In the short term, however, share performance is likely to depend on drilling results from the ongoing program, progress on technical studies, early plans for San Manuel and the company's ability to fund its plans on acceptable terms. Broader copper price trends, macroeconomic data and geopolitical developments will continue to shape sentiment toward developers, and volatility is likely to remain elevated until risk appetite improves.

Electrification, power grids and data centers are driving copper demand, highlighting the need for alternative sources such as tailings or fine-grained mining waste.
The looming copper supply gap won’t close through mine production alone. Part of the answer lies in processing waste that historical mining left behind.
Data from the University of Queensland’s Sustainable Minerals Institute estimates that approximately 13 billion metric tons of mine tailings are generated every year. Copper, in particular, has seen a bulk of tailings due to constant activity.
The University of Arizona said that the past century of major mining has generated an estimated 17.5 billion metric tons of copper tailings, with upwards of 200 million metric tons now added annually and “more to come” as more copper is mined.
In historical mining areas like the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), decades of activity have also left large volumes of copper tailings, calling for new technology that could change how these waste materials are processed and valued.
Canadian resource and extraction company CoTec Holdings (TSXV:CTH,OTCQX:CTHCF) answers through its joint venture with US-listed and DRC-focused Copper Intelligence (OTCID:CUAI), a partnership that combines the acquisition and advancement of copper tailings projects with modern processing technologies.
A study from S&P Global shows that overall copper demand will jump about 50 percent by 2040, rising to 42 million metric tons and potentially creating a 10 million metric ton supply deficit. Much of this is attributed to “the accelerating pace of electrification,” coupled with the emerging AI and defense sectors.
Demand from data centers alone is expected to reach up to 2.5 million metric tons by 2040, with copper employed for its signal transmission, power transfer and thermal control capacities.
Mining remains the primary source of copper and is currently providing the short-term supply. The Society for Mining, Metallurgy & Exploration notes that current mines are running out of ore or nearing exhaustion. New supply will also not meet the 2040 deadline, as the average time to bring a copper mine from discovery to production is 17.9 years.
S&P estimates that aggressive recycling could provide about a third of total copper needs by 2040, and the International Energy Agency said that it reduces new mine development needs by 40 percent by 2050. While these statistics seem promising, they point to the fact that adding recycling alone will not close the gap.
In 2021, Bloomberg reported that roughly 43 million metric tons of copper are sitting idle in waste dumps across mines worldwide. What makes tailings attractive, aside from global quantity, is that they no longer require time for exploration, or mining and crushing ore. The material is already sitting on the surface; what’s left is proper processing and management to unlock its value.
Tailings were deemed uneconomical in the past as the technology needed to process them was still inefficient. Demand at the time also did not call for a secondary source, and it only made sense for miners to exhaust resources to produce the highest grade possible and not extend efforts to re-crush or re-process waste.
In the DRC, state-owned Gécamines generated large volumes of copper tailings from industrial mining that began in the 1950s. Today, those tailings remain a defining feature of the Central African Copperbelt and include the Kolwezi tailings, which have led to ERG Africa’s Metalkol roan tailings reclamation project.
ERG states that Metalkol uses dredging and hydro-sluicing technology to recover tailings, which then uses high-pressure water to mobilize material. This offers a look at how modern technology creates advanced extraction and sustainable and cost-effective solutions, allowing miners to revisit tailings from the past.
Another example is Minera Valle Central (MVC) in Chile, which reprocesses materials into valuable commodities. Since 1992, MVC has partnered with state-owned Codelco to recover copper and molybdenum from both new and old tailings of El Teniente, the world’s largest underground copper mine. Powered by renewable energy, the process extracts minerals through water, which are crushed and separated from waste to make valuable portions float. The industry underlines that eco-friendly methods such as this also protect ecosystems, agriculture and community health.
Canadian company CoTec Holdings has built its copper strategy around the presence of tailings in historical mining jurisdictions like the DRC. The US Geological Survey records the DRC’s 2025 mine production at 3.2 million metric tons, making it the world’s second largest producer behind Chile. A concentration of this production comes from the Central African Copperbelt, one of the richest copper and cobalt provinces in the world.
CoTec finalized a joint venture agreement with Copper Intelligence in September 2026, under which it is building a framework for pursuing tailings opportunities across the DRC's historical copper districts. The joint venture will combine CoTec's technology with Copper Intelligence's on-the-ground resource execution experience following a staged approach, testing technologies on each project to control capital and ensure maximum results.
Copper demand will continue to grow, and mining and recycling supply is running out of ways to catch up. Modern technology is shifting the gaze toward tailings from historical jurisdictions, which can produce a secondary, additional source with less time and resources.
With its newly formed joint venture, planned acquisitions and staged approach, CoTec Holdings is tapping into this opportunity. The company offers a peek into how technology and proper execution could support copper supply with waste, building from the ground up.

Saudi oil company Aramco plans to increase the capacity of the East-West pipeline, also known as Petroline, from about 7 million to 10 million barrels per day. The expansion of the route, which makes it possible to transport oil bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, is expected to take two to three years, Fortune reports.
Route to the Red Sea
Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said the company is also conducting engineering studies on additional export routes. The approximately 750-mile pipeline runs from the Abqaiq processing hub near the Persian Gulf to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea.
Before the war began, the pipeline typically transported about 2 million barrels of oil per day. At the end of March, it reached its full capacity of 7 million barrels per day, with about 2 million barrels of this volume going to Saudi refineries rather than for export.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
Supply risks
Gilbert Metcalf, a lecturer at the MIT Sloan School of Management and former U.S. Treasury deputy assistant secretary for environment and energy, believes that if Saudi Arabia can increase pipeline flows to 10 million barrels per day, it could add about 2% of oil to the global market and somewhat lower prices. At the same time, he stressed the vulnerability of the pipeline and other oil infrastructure in the kingdom to drone and missile attacks, as well as uncertainty over available refining capacity.
Petroline has been attacked repeatedly this year. According to Kpler, following a drone strike on September 10, the pipeline was shut down as a precaution until September 22. The sea route via the port of Yanbu also involves risks in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait area, through which tankers heading south from the Red Sea pass.
According to Kpler, oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz averaged slightly less than 9 million barrels per day in September — about 44% of the February level. Metcalf noted that even an expansion of the Saudi pipeline may not reduce the global market's dependence on this strait.

However, the rebound does not guarantee a lasting recovery. Prices will depend on Indonesia’s production decisions, stainless steel demand, battery trends, and the growth of new supply.
LME Nickel Price Curve Signals Higher Future Prices
The LME nickel price curve shows that nickel prices are higher for contracts with longer delivery dates. Prices rise from around $15,900 per tonne for immediate delivery to approximately $18,400 per tonne for December 2029.
This upward trend suggests the market expects nickel prices to be higher in the future, although the curve reflects current market pricing rather than a guaranteed forecast.
Indonesia’s Production Cuts Could Tighten Supply
Indonesia’s nickel industry faces pressure from weaker selling prices, rising costs, and tighter mining quotas. These conditions have increased the incentive for producers to reconsider production levels.
Under its annual work plan and budget system, known as RKAB, the country approved a lower nickel ore production quota for 2026 than for 2025. The International Nickel Study Group (INSG) noted that Indonesia’s quota decisions consider supply and demand conditions. Applications for 2027 quotas are due by November 15, 2026.
Weather Disruptions and Weak Production Add to Supply Risks
Weather-related disruptions have added another supply risk. Bloomberg earlier reported that water shortages linked to El Niño forced nickel smelters at the Morowali Industrial Park to reduce nickel pig iron (NPI) production. The potential impact was estimated at 100,000 tonnes.
NPI is a lower-grade nickel product primarily used in stainless steel production. Reduced NPI output could tighten supply in that segment, while potential cuts at HPAL facilities could affect nickel intermediates used in battery manufacturing.
These developments could support prices if they lead to meaningful production losses. However, lower mining quotas and temporary operating disruptions do not automatically translate into a sustained global shortage, particularly when producers continue to expand processing capacity.
- IEA further added that low prices continued to hurt nickel production outside Indonesia, with mined output falling by over 10% and refined production declining by nearly 3%.
The Northern Miner reported that Chinese-backed projects in Indonesia have expanded capacity for both stainless steel and battery materials, adding to the challenge of balancing supply with demand.
INSG Forecasts Nickel Surplus in 2026 and 2027
Despite the recent price gains, the global nickel market is expected to remain in surplus, according to the INSG’s October outlook.
The intergovernmental group revised its 2026 forecast from a 32,000-tonne deficit in April to a 19,000-tonne surplus. The earlier projection would have marked the first annual supply shortfall since 2021.
The revision reflects stronger expected production growth than previously anticipated. Both supply and demand have increased in the group’s estimates, but production remains slightly ahead of consumption.
The INSG’s latest forecast is explained below in detail:
The forecasts suggest that the market surplus will narrow substantially in 2026 before expanding again in 2027. Although this year’s projected surplus is relatively small compared with 2025, it still indicates that expected production exceeds consumption.
The INSG also cautioned that its production estimates do not account for an adjustment factor for potential supply disruptions. Actual output could therefore differ from the forecast.
Stainless Steel and EV Battery Demand Remain Key Drivers
Nickel demand depends heavily on stainless steel manufacturing, with rechargeable batteries providing another important source of consumption.
According to the World Stainless Association, global stainless steel melt shop production increased 5% year over year in the first half of 2026. The INSG expects the sector to expand further in the second half of this year and throughout 2027.
Growth in stainless steel production could help absorb additional nickel supply. However, the outlook for electric vehicle (EV) batteries remains less certain.
IEA Forecast:
The IEA expects batteries to account for 30% of total nickel consumption by 2035, driving nearly two-thirds of demand growth. Demand is likely to come mainly from battery makers outside China, particularly in North America and Europe, where consumers favor long-range electric vehicles (EVs).
However, the growing adoption of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, which do not require nickel, could limit battery-grade nickel demand. Nickel-based batteries will remain important for some EV applications, but their adoption rate will influence how quickly new supply is absorbed.
Can Nickel Prices Sustain the Rebound?
Nickel’s rise above $16,000 per tonne shows how prices can react to expected production cuts. However, Indonesia’s producers have yet to agree on the proposed reductions, so actual supply cuts remain uncertain.
The INSG expects a small surplus of 19,000 tonnes in 2026, rising to 70,000 tonnes in 2027. This suggests oversupply risks will persist, especially if battery demand grows more slowly than expected.
For now, nickel prices will depend on actual production cuts, Indonesia’s mining quotas, and demand from stainless steel and battery makers. Without lower supply or stronger demand, the recent rally may be short-lived.

articles.title: Brent crude oil price rises amid Middle East tensions - Inspenet
articles.summary: Brent crude oil price rises amid Middle East tensions  Inspenet
articles.full_text:
He Brent crude oil price reached their highest level in more than five months on Friday, October 23, amid renewed tensions in the Middle East. Recent Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia have heightened concerns about potential disruptions to crude oil supplies from one of the world’s major producing regions.
At 10:06 GMT, Brent crude futures were up 1% at $114.31 a barrel, during the session, the price reached $114.72, its highest level since May 4. Meanwhile, West Texas Intermediate (WTI), the US benchmark, was up 1.7% at $101.12.
With this performance, Brent crude was on track to complete its third consecutive week of gains, with an increase of nearly 4%. WTI, on the other hand, was expected to close the week with a 0.3% decline.
Houthi attacks increase the risk to oil supplies
The situation in Saudi Arabia according to Reuters, Saudi Aramco ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on Thursday, keeping oil market operators on alert amid escalating clashes between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis.
One of the main concerns is related to Bab el-Mandeb, the strait that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. It is a strategic passage for maritime oil transport, so any disruption could delay deliveries and increase freight costs.
Adding to this situation are the high costs of maritime transport and the constant changes in trade routes.,Giovanni Staunovo, an analyst at UBS, warned that an escalation of the conflict could lead to further supply disruptions, a possibility that continues to put pressure on prices.
Why is the price of Brent crude oil rising?
The recent rise in Brent crude is primarily due to uncertainty surrounding oil availability on the international market. When attacks occur in producing regions or there are threats to shipping routes, buyers typically anticipate potential delays and seek to secure their supplies.
In this scenario, one of the big questions is how much oil could be affected and for how long operations would remain interrupted.
Linh Tran, an analyst at XS.com, explained that the duration and scope of any potential outages will be key in determining the risk premium the market is charging. If the attacks continue and affect deliveries, prices could remain under pressure for a longer period.
Furthermore, the increased cost of freight presents another challenge for refineries and international buyers, as it raises the cost of transporting crude oil from producing countries to their destinations.
A spill in the United Arab Emirates adds pressure to the sector
In parallel to the tensions in Saudi Arabia, authorities in the United Arab Emirates reported an oil spill off the coast of Umm Al Quwain.
The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment reported that the spill originated from a tanker, upon learning of the incident, authorities initiated containment efforts and assessments to determine its potential impact on the marine ecosystem.
Up to that point, there was no information on what caused the spill or which ship was involved, nor were there any elements that would allow the incident to be directly linked to the attacks recorded in Middle East.
Libya reduces its production due to the closure of an oil pipeline
Outside the Middle East, Libya’s oil industry is also facing difficulties, the closure of a valve on the pipeline connecting the Hamada and Tahara fields to the port of Zawiya has led to a reduction in production at both fields.
The situation was reported to Reuters by an official from Libya’s National Oil Corporation, however, no details were given about how much crude oil production had stopped or when operations might resume.
Although this incident is not linked to the conflict in Yemen, it represents another source of uncertainty for a market that closely monitors any event that could affect the global supply of oil.
Russian diesel heads to the United States amid rising crude oil prices
On the other hand, LSEG data revealed that a Maltese-flagged vessel was transporting 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel to New York.
The shipment is part of a broader opening in fuel trade, following an agreement between the United States and Russia to facilitate supply to international markets. As part of that agreement, Russia agreed to lift its own restrictions on diesel exports.
The measure aims to contribute to lower fuel prices, although its results will depend on the amount of product that reaches the market and how global availability evolves.
For now, the price of Brent crude continues to be influenced by uncertainty in the Middle East, the evolution of the attacks, the security of shipping routes, and the continuity of supplies will be key factors in market behavior during the coming sessions.

Kinder Morgan said its adjusted net income for the third quarter was up 22% compared to year-ago levels. The company added that it has a large backlog of projects that could enhance the natural gas sector even further.
Released Friday, October 23, 2026

Summary
Kinder Morgan said its adjusted net income for the third quarter was up 22% compared to year-ago levels. The company added that it has a large backlog of projects that could enhance the natural gas sector even further.
LNG the Main Driver
There's a project backlog worth more than $13 billion in just natural gas alone, Kinder Morgan said in announcing it could be expanding its portfolio even further.
Industrial Info Resources data show grassroot pipeline projects worth at least a half-billion dollars that are tied to Kinder Morgan in the U.S. natural gas sector. It's behind an interconnector that would run from Jefferson County in Texas to Cameron Parish in Louisiana, carrying around 1.3 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) of natural gas, data show.
On Wednesday, Kinder Morgan said its performance was lifted in large part by the natural gas sector. Adjusted net income attributable to Kinder Morgan in the third quarter was $729 million, 22% higher than the same period last year.
"Our natural gas business in particular is benefiting from increasing LNG (liquefied natural gas) exports, rising power demand, and industrial expansion and is capitalizing on significant opportunities for investment across our footprint," Executive Chairman Richard Kinder said in a statement.
LNG exports globally are under pressure from the conflict in the Middle East, where major suppliers Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are limited because of war-related damage to their energy infrastructure.
That leaves it to the United States, the world leader in LNG exports, to pick up the slack. The amount of feed gas supporting U.S.-sourced LNG continues to hover near record highs. In its NATGAS Today report for Thursday, Industrial Info found feed gas levels reached 19.45 billion cubic feet, some 1.5% above prior-day levels.
"Natural gas transport volumes were up 3% compared to the third quarter of 2025, primarily due to LNG deliveries on Tennessee Gas Pipeline (TGP) and increased demand for services on our Texas Intrastate system," Kinder Morgan President Dax Sanders said in a statement.
TGP alone is a massive network of interconnected pipe that runs from Texas all the way up the Atlantic Coast, Industrial Info data show.
Deep Bench for Kinder Morgan
Industrial Info is tracking several projects tied to the U.S. natural gas sector for Kinder Morgan. The largest project is the proposed Pascagoula terminal for exports of LNG from Louisiana.
Led by Gulf LNG Energy, the plant would have a design capacity of 5.75 million metric tons per annum if it's completed as planned.
Kinder Morgan also is working on an optimization project at Southern LNG Incorporated's Elba Island LNG export facility in Savannah, Georgia. The company is constructing a condensate plant and installing three new liquid nitrogen vaporizers, which are expected to boost the facility's liquefaction capacity by 400,000 metric tons per year to 2.9 million metric tons.
Kinder Morgan added that it was backing an industry surge with capital expansions. Some $660 million in expansion projects were placed into service during the second quarter, including the Gulf Coast Express pipeline that will send gas from the Permian shale basin to the South Texas coast.
On Thursday, the company added that it had a project backlog that could support another 5 Bcf/d in gas deliveries.
"The expansion project backlog at the end of the third quarter was $14.4 billion, up $4.7 billion from the second quarter of 2026, with $5.4 billion of additions net of $700 million in projects placed in service," Chief Executive Officer Kim Dang said.

articles.title: Koryx Copper Seeks Re-Rating as Upsized Haib PFS Nears Completion - Crux Investor
articles.summary: Koryx Copper Seeks Re-Rating as Upsized Haib PFS Nears Completion  Crux Investor
articles.full_text:
- Koryx Copper expects to publish the Haib PFS before the end of November 2026, and management expects it to beat the 2025 PEA substantially.
- Heap leaching has been removed, and the base case now crushes 48 Mtpa, with coarse particle flotation rejecting about 12 Mtpa of gangue.
- Agreements with NamPower and NamWater have defined the power and water routes, which reduces two long-standing infrastructure risks.
- Securing financing for expected capex of $1.5 billion to $2 billion is the key risk, and the company plans to address it through a strategic partner in 2027.
- Koryx trades at 0.24 times P/NAV against a developer median of 0.28 times, so a successful PFS could support a re-rating.
Copper development projects that combine scale, existing infrastructure and a credible path to construction are becoming harder to find. That scarcity sits at the centre of the investment case for Koryx Copper S.A. (TSXV:KRY), the Luxembourg-domiciled developer advancing the 100%-owned Haib Copper Project in southern Namibia. Speaking in London during LME Week, President & CEO Heye Daun said the company expects to publish its Pre-Feasibility Study (PFS) before the end of November 2026. He expects the results to be substantially better than the September 2025 Preliminary Economic Assessment (PEA). Koryx has spent two years reworking a large, low-grade porphyry deposit with a long exploration history. The PFS is the document that will show whether that technical work produces a project that lenders and strategic partners can back. The company is pitching the study as the trigger for closing a valuation gap that its own peer benchmarking puts below the developer median.
From Turnaround to Pre-Feasibility
Haib is one of only a few Paleoproterozoic porphyry copper deposits in the world, carrying molybdenum and gold credits alongside copper. It has been explored by Falconbridge, Rio Tinto and Teck over several decades, and more than 160,000 metres of drilling has been completed on the property since the 1970s. Daun’s team took control of Koryx in 2024 and set out a technical strategy of right-sizing and optimising the project, then making it bigger and better. The same group previously built and sold Auryx Gold to B2Gold for $180 million in 2011 and Osino Resources to Shanjin International Gold (formerly Yintai Gold) for C$368 million in 2024, both Namibian projects.
The recently completed infill programme of more than 55,000 metres was designed to lift grade and convert Inferred material into the Indicated category ahead of the PFS. The March 2026 Mineral Resource Estimate (MRE) stands at 744 million tonnes Indicated at 0.28% copper (0.32% copper equivalent, or CuEq) and 579 million tonnes Inferred at 0.24% copper (0.28% CuEq). Daun was measured about the impact of individual intercepts. He noted that a block of roughly 1.5 billion tonnes is hard to shift on average grade. He pointed instead to higher-grade pockets the mine plan will target. Recent holes include 74 metres at 0.61% CuEq, including 8 metres at 1.74% CuEq.
Interview with Heye Daun, President & CEO, Koryx Copper
A Simpler, Larger Flowsheet
The most significant change since the PEA is the processing route. Daun explained that the original thesis of sulphide heap leaching works in the laboratory but is not credible at industrial scale. Test work confirmed that Haib needs to be a milling and flotation operation. The interim PFS update published on 8 October confirmed that heap leaching is no longer expected to form part of the PFS base case, with all production now coming through the mill.
A debottlenecking study by lead engineer DRA Global has set PFS base case crushing throughput at 48 million tonnes per annum (Mtpa). Coarse particle flotation (CPF) is expected to reject roughly 12 Mtpa of coarse gangue grading 0.05% copper before the main flotation circuit. That leaves 36 Mtpa of higher-grade feed for a hybrid circuit of conventional tank cells and Jameson cells. The comparable PEA case was a 28 Mtpa mill alongside 7 Mtpa of heap leaching. The company has also selected a single tailings storage facility site from nine candidates, capable of holding the full life-of-mine total of about 1.15 billion tonnes.
The Baseline to Beat
The September 2025 PEA set the benchmark. It outlined an after-tax net present value (NPV) of $1.351 billion at an 8% discount rate and a copper price of $4.30 per pound. It also showed an after-tax internal rate of return (IRR) of 20.1%, development capital of $1.559 billion and a payback period of 3.9 years. Average payable copper production was 92,000 tonnes per annum over the first ten years, across a 23-year mine life. C1 cash costs were $1.81 per pound and all-in sustaining costs (AISC) were $2.05 per pound over the same period.
Daun would not give PFS numbers ahead of publication. He said final recovery and drill results were due within a week. He expects annual copper output to be well over 100,000 tonnes. He indicated that capital expenditure would land somewhere between $1.5 billion and $2 billion. He added that a large share of the capital estimate already rests on supplier quotes rather than factoring, closer to definitive feasibility study (DFS) practice.
That emphasis on estimate quality reflects who the study is really written for. Daun said retail share buyers drive the share price day to day, but
“the ultimate test is the corporates or the project financiers, the banks, the real money, the big money that comes in to build this mine. They focus on quality.”
Infrastructure & Permitting
Daun said power was once seen as Haib’s main constraint but is now de-risked. Electricity will be drawn through the Namibian grid but sourced from South Africa, where he said Eskom has surplus capacity in the nearby Northern Cape. Koryx has signed a Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) with NamPower. The planned supply is a 68-kilometre, double-circuit 220 kilovolt line from the Harib substation, supplemented by solar photovoltaic generation and battery storage.
Water will come from the Orange River, selected as the lowest-cost option, via a single abstraction point about 9 kilometres south of the mine and an off-channel storage reservoir. Koryx has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with NamWater. Daun put the water scheme’s capital cost at about $150 million. He said a materially larger scheme would require another round of permitting, which he described as an option for a future owner rather than a current constraint.
On permitting, the Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA) and Environmental Management Plan supporting the Environmental Clearance Certificate were submitted to the Ministry of Environment, Forestry and Tourism on 19 August and 4 September 2026. The company is planning for a review period of up to six months. Daun said broad support from government, local communities and the wider population helps Namibian projects move through permitting faster.
Closing the Valuation Gap
Daun was direct about where he believes the market has mispriced the company.
“...we will put on the table a world-class, simple, long-life, low-cost, scalable... copper mine. Potential copper mine. That should be valued at a share price that’s substantially higher than ours is currently.”
The company’s own benchmarking places Koryx at 0.24 times price to net asset value (P/NAV), against a copper developer median of 0.28 times. At C$3.41 on 15 September 2026, the fully diluted market capitalisation was about C$460 million. Five research analysts cover the stock, with published targets ranging from $4.50 to $8.00.
Daun identified project financing uncertainty as the largest obstacle to a re-rating. The steps planned after the PFS target that directly: financing certainty, endorsement from credible technical groups and the introduction of a strategic investor. The indicative schedule shows the DFS, major permits and a review of strategic options and project financing running through 2027. A front-end engineering phase and a three-year construction period would follow, with first copper production estimated in 2031.
Investment Thesis for Koryx Copper
- The PFS, due before the end of November 2026, is the next major catalyst, and management expects results to be substantially better than the PEA.
- Removing heap leaching and adding CPF and Jameson cells has simplified the flowsheet while raising base case throughput to 48 Mtpa.
- Power and water routes are now defined through agreements with NamPower and NamWater, reducing two historical infrastructure risks.
- Project financing for capital expenditure of $1.5 billion to $2 billion remains the key risk, and investors should monitor progress on a strategic partner during 2027.
- Investors should track the Environmental Clearance Certificate decision, which is a condition for the Mining Licence the company has applied for.
- The stock trades at 0.24 times P/NAV against a developer median of 0.28 times, leaving room for a re-rating if the PFS and financing steps deliver.
Macro Thematic Analysis
Copper demand is being pulled by electrification, grid investment and data centre build-out, while new supply has struggled to keep pace. Large discoveries are rare, and many existing projects face long permitting timelines or water and political risk. That leaves a short list of development assets capable of producing more than 100,000 tonnes of copper a year.
Daun said one of the clearest signals of market tightness is in treatment and refining charges, the fees smelters receive to process concentrate. He described them as deeply negative, which indicates strong competition for copper concentrate.
His view of what this means for strategic buyers is clear.
“...fundamentally speaking with supply and demand situations extremely positive for copper, and that’s why the corporates and companies that we meet and that we talk to, they all have copper right up at the top of their strategic ambitions.”
